en: Gathering all of them in great numbers.
Then, famed for his fearsome presence,
He was khan of Meke-Dilde.
He went in to the sultan and received a blessing.
Toward the khakans' Beijing,
His seething army rode out.
When he had gathered the people,
He traveled on that journey.
When he arrived at Karkyra,
Gathering countless stones in his hands,
He set them up as a marker.
Without fighting or disputing,
When he entered Beijing,
‘Beijing, which even the holy one cannot touch—
Turn back without overrunning it.
You have come desiring something;
I shall give you what you wish.
Return as a relative through marriage,’ he said.
Then, however many troops there were,
They had spread throughout Beijing.
The great khan of the khakans
Said, ‘Whichever wife you desire,
Take her away, warrior.’
Of those under thirty-three,
He left no married woman at home;
Of those above seventeen,
He left no maiden in his city.
The Muslims who had gone to Beijing—
He assembled the Muslim army.
The mighty warrior, Beijing's great khan:
‘Muslim, you have come as a guest.
Take one if she pleases you,’ he said.
To those people who had come,
With Medirese at their head,
He gave his daughters.
When their king did so,
Those who had come took wives.
Before Kuroogon turned back,
Some had already had children.
Samarkand's blue stone
Had first been Chinese land.
Then Medirese, the true beauty,
Asked for it as her own allotted property.
Then, as I recall, he took many lands.
To perdition with the lands he took!
Then, in the city of Beijing,
The Salaalyk Kyrgyz people remained.
Mother, from the great city of Misir down below,
The troops on this side went forth,
In the time of Khan Kuroogon,
Going in numbers, not sparing their lives.
Then, as they took wives,
Beijing resounded with commotion.
Mother, let me tell the tale.
Over eighteen thousand worlds
He had passed his life as king.
Leave him aside—even Holy Ali, where is he?
Seen today, gone tomorrow,
Thus this dung of a world keeps deceiving us!
When I see this broad Ak-Chii,
Thick embers fall within my breast!
Mother, I come fleeing to Bukhara.
The one whom I counted on,
The leopard sultan, is gone as well!
Amir-Temir, Kuroogon—
God has taken him away.
Born endowed with sanctity,
Let me tell how I prospered.
Listen, my saintly mother.
Here in Bukhara,
Let me tell how I grew up.
As a human, a wretched soul,
Let me tell how I was born.
In Bukhara, my father Temir Khan,
Without seeing a son in this world,
Had seen twelve daughters.
Exacting bride-prices, taking marriage payments,
He gave the twelve to twelve khans.
My stricken father lamented,
And as the thirteenth one,
He saw me, the wretched one.
‘Though my child is a daughter,
I would not exchange her for sixty sons,’ he said.
He slaughtered a mare for my feast
And named me Kanykei the Beautiful.
For good fortune he hung an amulet about my neck
And raised me with affection.
He oiled and braided my hair
And cherished me like his faith.
His good fortune grew and overflowed.
When I reached the age of two,
My mother gave birth to Ismail.
‘The beauty among the dark-complexioned,
The radiant one among Muslims,
My precious child,’ he said.
Holding me beyond all measure,
Cherishing me when I was a girl,
My father heeded my words.
When I reached the age of seven,
‘My child will be accomplished,’ she said.
My wretched, ruined mother
Hung a ruby set in gold about my neck.
All Bukhara, the Sart people,
Raised me with affection.
I was a little girl,
My age had not passed twelve.
When I was a beauty among women,
When I was a playful young girl,
Turning my winged steed's head,
In those days, standing there at play,
To the royal realm of Bukhara
I gave stern orders.
Those who answered back
I slaughtered like sheep.
In my own father's city of Bukhara,
I did as I pleased.
Exerting power beyond all bounds,
Those of my own age—
Forcing tribute and taxes,
I gathered the girls of Bukhara.
My fine hair as thick as a saddle-girth
I bound snugly upon my crown.
Eighty girls on this side,
Eighty girls on that side,
Riding pacing horses without jolting,
Wearing silk coats draped over their shoulders,
My gold cap adorned with flowers
Shining brightly upon my head,
Taking girls as my companions,
I would go on outings.
In my maiden days, I, the wretched one,
Ruled this broad Bukhara.
At times, playing and exploring the land,
My many stewards who tended horses,
Servants who spread the tents,
Slaughtered mares by day,
Slaughtered yearlings where we spent the night.
Bukhara's coursers
I had tethered along the hitching line.
Well-fed lamb, sweet head that I was,
I, the wretched one, stirred up merry outings,
Every place where I passed
I filled with abundance.
Leaving Bukhara without holding back,
Traveling for six days,
For an outing, little creature that I was,
I used to come to this place.
Kanykei's Ken-Kolchuk—
Kolchuk, blessed with every good fortune.
In its yearly season, poor soul that I am,
I used to come for an outing.
When I arrived in those days,
My precious mother,
I would attain my desire.
Eighty young wives, eighty maidens—
In my playful girlhood,
Oh, mother, listen:
I used to play and laugh in this place.
Ken-Kolchuk that lies in view,
Mother, Kolchuk blessed with every good fortune.
There is writing upon the birch;
There is the name of unfortunate Kanykei.
There is writing upon the poplar;
There is the name of your ocean-like child, Kanykei.
A grove of plane trees surrounds Kolchuk.
Where this unfortunate woman sat on her outings,
There is the golden throne I mounted at play.
Showing the girls discipline,
Those dear days when I went about like that!
Snug beneath that throne—
If I speak, my words to Allah are a lament—
Kanykei had sent to fetch from Bukhara
And had laid beneath the throne
A huge carpet.
Let me tell you of that carpet:
A huge carpet with golden patterns,
If cast in water for forty years,
Not the least of its edge would fade.
If soaked in water for eighty years,
Not a strip of its edge would fade.
Its weft was silk and gold,
Its warp of fine, costly thread.
Laid before the throne,
The huge carpet with golden patterns
Could not be found though sought far afield,
An exceedingly costly great carpet.
The golden throne upon it—
In my playful childhood,
Kanykei, this ruined woman,
Those were the days when I played there.
Let us go and see Kolchuk,
My precious mother,
And then let us reach Bukhara.
Kanykei's Ken-Kolchuk,
Kolchuk, blessed with every good fortune.
A golden throne stood at its edge,
A grove of plane trees all around.
Such, in her maiden days,
Was Kanykei's khanship.
Not even a winged crow could come and go,
By the decree her khan had issued.
The warrior woman Kanykei
Had made a gift of Ken-Kolchuk.
When they came to Ken-Kolchuk,
Its lake had dried up.
The grove of plane trees all around
Had withered completely.
The palace built there, the cool resting place,
Had utterly collapsed.
The golden throne and huge carpet—
The people of Bukhara had plundered them.
Oh, grief-bringing world, may you never prosper!
Thus God had struck it down.
At the lake and its poplars
Kanykei now gazed.
Unable to contain herself, that dear soul,
Kanykei, the falcon-woman,
Could not stay silent and began to speak:
“Oh, my precious mother,
Even two days in Bukhara
We shall not lodge before we die.
Upon this earth, we poor creatures
Shall find no room and die.
We were well-fed; our crest-fat has gone,
And we shall become lean.
There are no people here to give us cheer.
Mother, we shall become destitute!
This Ken-Kolchuk standing here,
Kolchuk, blessed with every good fortune—
My lake has dried up.
My precious mother,
What can this mean?
Do not leave this fierce woman sobbing;
Mother, interpret this occurrence for me.
My prophet-like sacred mother,
My precious mother,
My fortune has failed to blossom.
Mother, my affairs have been buried!
Interpret this state of mine;
Mother, what can it mean?
When I went about in those days,
When I came on an outing,
My plane trees used to put forth leaves.
‘It is truly a sacred shrine,’ they said;
The people bowed in reverence.
That great city of Bukhara looming dark—
‘It is endowed with sanctity,’ they said,
And slaughtered great numbers of their livestock.
‘Kanykei's Ken-Kolchuk,
Kolchuk, blessed with every good fortune,’
The people used to call it.
Beneath this plane tree,
When a dervish came, he ate his fill.
‘May fierce Kanykei never be humiliated,’
He would give his blessing.
My lake has dried up;
